title: Making retries safe: idempotency keys, backoff, and dead-letter queues
description: Networks fail in the middle of requests, so real systems retry, and retries are where duplicate charges and lost messages come from. Learn the difference between at-least-once, at-most-once, and 'exactly-once' delivery, and why the last one can't exist over a lossy network. You'll also cover idempotency keys and server-side dedup, exponential backoff with jitter, which requests are safe to retry, the Two Generals' Problem, and poison messages, plus how to retry a payment without charging the customer twice.

questions.title: Which delivery guarantee does this broker behavior describe?
questions.description: A message broker keeps redelivering a message until the consumer acknowledges it. If an acknowledgment is lost in transit, the broker sends the same message again.

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but the acknowledgment is lost on the way back, so the sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost ack. It can only retry or not retry. Three lanes then show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane, and it does not get around that result.
images.caption: Redelivering until acked is the middle lane.

options.text: At-least-once
At-most-once
Exactly-once
Best-effort (fire-and-forget)

questions.explanation:
Delivery guarantees trade off two failures: losing messages and duplicating them.

- **At-most-once** sends once and never retries. A lost message is gone for good, but you never see a duplicate. Each message arrives 0 or 1 times.
- **At-least-once** retries until the consumer acknowledges. Nothing gets lost, but when an acknowledgment is lost, the broker resends a message the consumer already handled. Each message arrives 1 or more times.
- **Exactly-once** means every message arrives once and only once. Over an unreliable network, no delivery protocol can guarantee that (see the Two Generals' Problem).

The broker in this question redelivers until it gets an ack and resends when an ack is lost. That's the textbook definition of at-least-once. It's also why at-least-once systems need idempotent consumers: duplicates will happen, so the consumer has to handle them.

questions.title: Which design delivers the achievable version of 'exactly-once'?
questions.description: A senior engineer says: 'Exactly-once *delivery* is impossible, but exactly-once *processing* is achievable.'

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but the acknowledgment is lost on the way back, so the sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost ack. It can only retry or not retry. Three lanes then show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane, and it does not get around that result.
images.caption: At-least-once plus dedup is the green lane.

options.text: At-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing (dedup) on the consumer
At-most-once delivery plus a faster, more reliable network so nothing is lost
A two-phase commit that makes the network channel itself perfectly reliable
Disabling retries so every message is transmitted exactly one time

questions.explanation:
No protocol can guarantee that a message crosses an unreliable network exactly once, because the sender can never be sure the message or its ack arrived. So real systems use at-least-once delivery, which retries and accepts duplicates. Then the receiver makes duplicates harmless with **idempotent processing or deduplication**, so each effect happens once. People call the result **effectively-once** or **exactly-once processing**.

Why the other options fail:
- A faster network makes loss less likely but never impossible, so at-most-once still drops messages.
- Two-phase commit coordinates a transaction across participants. It can't make a lossy channel reliable.
- Turning off retries gives you at-most-once, which loses the message on the first failure.

Kafka's 'exactly-once semantics' only holds inside Kafka's own transactional log, using an idempotent producer and transactions. It can't make an outside side effect, like a card charge at a payment provider, happen exactly once.
questions.references: [Confluent: Exactly-Once Semantics Are Possible in Apache Kafka](https://www.confluent.io/blog/exactly-once-semantics-are-possible-heres-how-apache-kafka-does-it/)

questions.title: What does the Two Generals' Problem establish?
questions.description: Two allied generals must attack at the same time to win. They can only coordinate through messengers, who might be captured crossing enemy territory.

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but the acknowledgment is lost on the way back, so the sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost ack. It can only retry or not retry. Three lanes then show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane, and it does not get around that result.
images.caption: The closing note sums up the result.

options.text: Two parties communicating over an unreliable channel can never *guarantee* agreement using a finite number of messages
Agreement is guaranteed as long as at least three acknowledgments are exchanged
TCP fully solves the problem by retransmitting any lost segment
The problem disappears once both parties share a synchronized clock

questions.explanation:
The **Two Generals' Problem** shows that two parties can't be certain they agree when any message might be lost. General A sends 'attack at dawn'. To know it arrived, A needs an acknowledgment. The ack can be lost too, so B needs an acknowledgment of the acknowledgment, and so on forever. No finite exchange makes both sides certain the other will act.

That's why exactly-once delivery is a myth, and why every system has to pick a risk:
- Stop retrying and risk losing the message (at-most-once).
- Keep retrying and risk duplicates (at-least-once).

Why the other options are wrong: no fixed number of acks ends the regress, so three is no safer than two. TCP doesn't solve it either. It retransmits and uses timeouts, but a connection can still die after the data arrives and before the ack gets back, which leaves the sender unsure. A shared clock tells the generals when to attack. It says nothing about whether the message arrived.

questions.title: Which HTTP methods are idempotent?
questions.description: RFC 9110 calls a method *idempotent* when sending the same request many times has the same effect on server state as sending it once. Select **all** that apply.

images.alt: Five steps. A client sends POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc-123. The client generates the key itself, one per logical operation. The charge succeeds and the server stores the key with the response. The connection drops before the response arrives, so the client doesn't know whether it charged the customer. The client retries the identical request with the same key. The server finds the key and replays the stored response without charging again. A card lists what the stored record must hold: the response, a request fingerprint so the same key with a different body is rejected, and an expiry, since after a 24-hour window the key counts as new. Six chips name the methods RFC 9110 defines as idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not among them.
images.caption: The six chips come straight from RFC 9110.

options.text: `GET`
`PUT`
`DELETE`
`POST`
`PATCH`

questions.explanation:
RFC 9110 lists `PUT`, `DELETE`, and all safe methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`) as idempotent. So `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are correct here, and `POST` and `PATCH` are not.

A few details worth knowing:
- Idempotent and safe mean different things. `GET` is safe because it only reads. `PUT` and `DELETE` change state, but they're still idempotent: writing the same full representation twice, or deleting the same resource twice, leaves the server in the same state as doing it once.
- `DELETE` stays idempotent even if the second call returns `404`. Idempotency is about the effect on server state (the resource is gone), not about getting the same status code.
- `POST` is neither safe nor idempotent. Two `POST /charges` calls create two charges. `PATCH` isn't guaranteed to be idempotent either: a relative patch like 'add 100 to balance' applied twice adds 200.

So retrying a plain `POST` is dangerous and needs an idempotency key, while retrying a `GET` is always fine.

questions.title: What should the server do when the same idempotency key arrives again?
questions.description: A mobile app sends `POST /charges` with the header `Idempotency-Key: abc-123`. The charge succeeds, but the connection drops before the response arrives, so the app retries with the **same** key. The server has already processed `abc-123`.

images.alt: Five steps. A client sends POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc-123. The client generates the key itself, one per logical operation. The charge succeeds and the server stores the key with the response. The connection drops before the response arrives, so the client doesn't know whether it charged the customer. The client retries the identical request with the same key. The server finds the key and replays the stored response without charging again. A card lists what the stored record must hold: the response, a request fingerprint so the same key with a different body is rejected, and an expiry, since after a 24-hour window the key counts as new. Six chips name the methods RFC 9110 defines as idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not among them.
images.caption: Step 5: find the key, replay the response, charge nothing.

options.text: Return the stored response from the first request, without charging again
Process a fresh charge, since the retry arrives on a new TCP connection
Reject the retry with a 4xx error and discard the original charge data
Charge the customer again, then immediately issue an automatic refund

questions.explanation:
An idempotency key makes an unsafe `POST` safe to retry. On the first request, the server runs the charge and saves the key together with the status code and response body. When a retry arrives with the same key, the server returns the saved result instead of running the charge again. The customer pays once, and the client finally gets its response.

```ts
const cached = await store.get(idempotencyKey);
if (cached) return cached.response;            // retry → replay stored result

const response = await charge(req);            // first time → do the work
await store.set(idempotencyKey, { response }); // persist key → result
return response;
```

The wrong options are real anti-patterns. A new TCP connection tells you nothing about whether the work already happened. Rejecting the retry and throwing away the charge data means the client can never learn the outcome. Charging and then refunding shows the customer two transactions. If the original request is still running when the retry arrives, the server should answer `409 Conflict` instead of charging again.

questions.title: Which statements about a correct idempotency-key design are true?
questions.description: A team is adding idempotency keys to a payments API. Select **all** that apply.

images.alt: Five steps. A client sends POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc-123. The client generates the key itself, one per logical operation. The charge succeeds and the server stores the key with the response. The connection drops before the response arrives, so the client doesn't know whether it charged the customer. The client retries the identical request with the same key. The server finds the key and replays the stored response without charging again. A card lists what the stored record must hold: the response, a request fingerprint so the same key with a different body is rejected, and an expiry, since after a 24-hour window the key counts as new. Six chips name the methods RFC 9110 defines as idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not among them.
images.caption: The card at the bottom lists the whole contract.

options.text: The client must reuse the same key when **retrying** a payment, but generate a new key for each **distinct** payment
The server should persist a key→result mapping so a retried request returns the original result without re-charging
Using one constant key for every request is fine, because the server deduplicates anyway
Adding an idempotency key reclassifies `POST` as a *safe* method under the HTTP spec

questions.explanation:
An idempotency key identifies one logical operation, and both sides have a job:
- The client generates a fresh key (a UUID, for example) for each distinct payment and sends that same key on every retry of it. That's how the server tells a retry of payment X from a brand-new payment.
- The server durably stores `key → {status, body}` and replays it on repeats, so the side effect runs at most once.

Why the false options fail:
- With one constant key for everything, the server would treat every payment as a duplicate of the first and drop real charges. Keys must be unique per operation, not per client.
- Safe and idempotent are different properties. Safe methods only read (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`). An idempotency key makes a `POST` safe to retry, but the `POST` still changes state, so it never becomes a safe method in the spec's sense.

questions.title: How many seconds does the client spend waiting in total?
questions.description: A client retries with exponential backoff. It waits 1 second before the first retry and doubles the wait each time (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …). It gives up after 5 retries.
questions.explanation:
The waits add up to `1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31` seconds. The first *n* doublings starting at 1 always sum to `2^n − 1`, so five retries give `2^5 − 1 = 31`.

That fast growth is the point of exponential backoff. A struggling server gets more and more time to recover instead of being hit at a fixed interval. The cost is latency: by the fifth retry, the client has waited half a minute. That's why production clients also set a maximum delay (a cap) and a retry limit or overall deadline, so the wait can't grow forever.
questions.references: [AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

questions.title: Why add jitter to backoff?
questions.description: A thousand clients hit an overloaded service and all fail at the same moment. They all use the same exponential backoff.

images.alt: Five backoff steps for a 100 ms base with no jitter: attempt 0 at 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, and attempt 4 highlighted at 1600 ms. Below are two lanes. Without jitter, every client retries at the same instant, marked thundering herd. With jitter, the same marks spread across the interval. Two cards contrast 429 Too Many Requests, meaning this client is over its own quota, with 503 Service Unavailable, meaning the upstream is shedding load for everyone. A note says Retry-After takes only delay-seconds or an HTTP-date.
images.caption: Jitter spreads the retries across the interval, so there's no single spike.

options.text: Their retries stay in sync and arrive together as a 'thundering herd' that overloads the service again; jitter randomizes the delays so retries spread out
Backoff delays grow without bound; jitter imposes the maximum-delay cap
The clients give up too early; jitter increases the total number of retries
The server cannot tell retries apart from new requests; jitter tags each retry with a unique id

questions.explanation:
Exponential backoff spaces out one client's retries, but it doesn't stop clients from retrying together. If everyone failed at the same moment and waits the same `1s, 2s, 4s…`, they all retry at the same instants. Those synchronized spikes, known as a thundering herd, knock the recovering service back down. Jitter adds randomness to each delay, so retries spread out over time and the server gets a load it can handle.

The wrong options mix up jitter with other settings. The cap limits the maximum delay. The retry limit or deadline limits how many attempts happen. Telling retries apart from new requests is the job of idempotency keys. In AWS's experiments, adding jitter cut both server contention and the total time clients needed to finish.

questions.title: What sleep time does full jitter use instead of the baseline?
questions.description: In AWS's backoff study, the baseline delay for attempt *n* is `min(cap, base * 2^n)`.

options.text: `random_between(0, min(cap, base * 2^n))`
`min(cap, base * 2^n) + random_between(0, base)`
`2 * min(cap, base * 2^n)`
`random_between(min(cap, base * 2^n), 2 * min(cap, base * 2^n))`

questions.explanation:
Full jitter drops the fixed delay and sleeps a random amount between zero and the capped exponential bound:

```py
sleep = random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** n))
```

Two clients on the same attempt can wait very different amounts, so they rarely retry together. The same study compares two other strategies:
- **Equal jitter** keeps half the delay fixed: `temp = min(cap, base * 2^n); sleep = temp/2 + random(0, temp/2)`.
- **Decorrelated jitter** grows from the previous sleep: `sleep = min(cap, random(base, prev_sleep * 3))`.

AWS found that full jitter and decorrelated jitter worked best, with the fewest client calls and the shortest completion time. The wrong options add a little randomness on top of a fixed delay, so clients stay mostly in sync.

questions.title: Which request is safe to retry blindly?
questions.description: Your HTTP client retries automatically after a network timeout and sends **no** idempotency key. "Safe to retry blindly" means repeating the request can't change server state more than the first call did.

images.alt: Five steps. A client sends POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc-123. The client generates the key itself, one per logical operation. The charge succeeds and the server stores the key with the response. The connection drops before the response arrives, so the client doesn't know whether it charged the customer. The client retries the identical request with the same key. The server finds the key and replays the stored response without charging again. A card lists what the stored record must hold: the response, a request fingerprint so the same key with a different body is rejected, and an expiry, since after a 24-hour window the key counts as new. Six chips name the methods RFC 9110 defines as idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not among them.
images.caption: Without a key, only the methods on the six chips are safe to repeat.

options.text: `GET /orders/42` to fetch an order's current status
`POST /transfers` to create a new money transfer
`POST /charges` to charge the customer's card
`PATCH /accounts/7` with body `{ "balance": "+100" }` to add 100 to the balance

questions.explanation:
`GET` is both safe (it only reads) and idempotent, so retrying it any number of times can't change server state. The other three change state again on every retry:
- `POST /transfers` and `POST /charges` create a new transfer or charge per call, so a retry does it twice.
- The relative `PATCH` ('add 100') is the classic non-idempotent write. Applied twice, it adds 200. A full-replacement `PUT` that sets `balance = 500` would be idempotent. The relative change is what breaks it.

You can always retry reads. Retry writes only after you've made them idempotent, usually with an idempotency key and server-side dedup.

questions.title: What's the most likely outcome of retrying 30 hours later?
questions.description: An API keeps idempotency keys for 24 hours to deduplicate retries. A client's request fails, the phone stays offline, and 30 hours later the client retries the *same* charge with the same key.

images.alt: Five steps. A client sends POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc-123. The client generates the key itself, one per logical operation. The charge succeeds and the server stores the key with the response. The connection drops before the response arrives, so the client doesn't know whether it charged the customer. The client retries the identical request with the same key. The server finds the key and replays the stored response without charging again. A card lists what the stored record must hold: the response, a request fingerprint so the same key with a different body is rejected, and an expiry, since after a 24-hour window the key counts as new. Six chips name the methods RFC 9110 defines as idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not among them.
images.caption: After the window, the stored record is gone, so the key looks new.

options.text: The key has already expired, so the server treats the retry as a new request and may charge the customer a second time
The server recognizes the key forever and returns the original charge
The retry is rejected with an error because the key is older than the window
The API automatically detects and refunds the resulting duplicate charge

questions.explanation:
Servers don't keep dedup records forever. They keep them for a dedup window with a TTL. Stripe, for example, prunes idempotency keys after about 24 hours. A retry that arrives after the key is gone looks brand new, so the charge can run again.

What this means in practice:
- Retries have to finish within the dedup window, so size your backoff and deadlines to fit.
- If retries can be delayed for days (an offline phone, a job stuck in a queue), a short server window isn't enough. You need durable client-side keys plus reconciliation, or a dedup store that keeps keys longer.

The wrong options assume the window is infinite, that expiry produces a clean error (usually the retry just looks like a new request), or that the system refunds duplicates on its own. A finite TTL guarantees none of these.

questions.title: What is the queue for repeatedly-failing messages called?
questions.description: A consumer keeps failing on one malformed message. The broker uses at-least-once delivery, so it redelivers this **poison message** over and over, and healthy messages pile up behind it. The usual fix is to move the message to a separate queue after a set number of failed attempts. Answer with three words or the acronym.
questions.explanation:
A poison message (or 'poison pill') fails every processing attempt, because of bad data, a schema mismatch, or a consumer bug. Under at-least-once redelivery it loops forever and can block every message behind it, which is called head-of-line blocking. The standard fix is a **dead-letter queue (DLQ)**. After a set number of failed attempts, the broker moves the message there. The main queue keeps flowing, and engineers can inspect, fix, or replay the message later.

This is also why retries need a limit. If you retry forever, one bad message can stall the pipeline for good. A DLQ, plus an alert on how many messages it holds, turns an endless loop into a backlog you can see and work through.
